meta.title: Engine
meta.description: The Ordo engine is written in Rust. Give it JSON, it runs your rules step by step and returns the result with the full path it took. Run it as a server or embed it in a program or a browser.

hero.title: Where the rules run
hero.subtitle: At the core of Ordo is a rule engine written in Rust. Give it JSON and it walks through your rules step by step, then returns the result and why each step went the way it did.

run.caption: The refund routing rules from the jev-routing rule pack, run on four real messages. The Jev answers came from typesafe/jev-1.13 on 2026-10-13; results match ordo trace.

steps.title: A rule is a chain of steps
steps.desc: A ruleset has one entry step. Each step looks at the input and picks the next step, until it reaches an end step. Rules are JSON or YAML files you can review in your repository.

kinds.name: Decision
kinds.desc: Checks conditions in order, takes the first one that holds, otherwise the default.

kinds.name: Decision table
kinds.desc: One rule per row, matched column by column. Good when there are many thresholds and combinations.

kinds.name: Action
kinds.desc: Computes new values and stores them for later steps.

kinds.name: Terminal
kinds.desc: Returns a result code, a message and output fields.

pipeline.title: Conditions are compiled before they run
pipeline.desc: Each condition is parsed once, when the rules load. Every execution after that runs compiled bytecode and never touches the string again.

stages.name: Parse
stages.desc: Read into a syntax tree. Once at load time, 1 to 2 µs.

stages.name: Optimize
stages.desc: Work out what can be computed ahead of time and drop branches that can't be reached.

stages.name: Bytecode
stages.desc: Compiled to register bytecode and run by a VM. Two conditions joined with && take about 80 ns.

stages.name: JIT
stages.desc: In a Rust program that declares its input types, purely numeric expressions can be compiled to machine code, about 8 ns. The server and the browser run bytecode.

pipeline.optNote: Nothing here can be computed ahead of time. Had it said amount > 100 * 2, it would become amount > 200.
pipeline.jitNote: This one compares a string, so it stays as bytecode. Purely numeric expressions such as score * 0.6 + bonus * 0.4 are the ones that go to the JIT.

speed.title: Under a microsecond per rule
speed.desc: A rule with four branches runs in about 573 ns. Inside a business request, most of the time goes to the network, not the rules.
speed.chartTitle: Same four-branch rule, time per execution
speed.baseline: For reference, a plain Rust if/else takes 3.5 ns

stats.label: HTTP requests per second, one instance, 200 concurrent
rule executions per second in batch

speed.note: Measured on an Apple M1 Pro on 2026-03-11. Other hardware and rules will give other numbers.

correct.title: Exact numbers, clear errors
correct.desc: Rules decide money and limits. A rounding error or a missing field can quietly send a request down the wrong branch. Below is real output from the CLI.

items.title: Exact decimals for money
items.desc: Declare a field as decimal, or wrap a value in decimal(), and arithmetic is exact base 10.

items.title: Input is checked first
items.desc: A rule declares the fields it needs and their types. If one is missing or has the wrong type, you get an error instead of the default branch.

lines.out: Invalid input: order.amount: required field is missing
Invalid input: jev.intent.confidence: expected number, got string

items.title: Rules come with tests
items.desc: Test cases live next to the rules and run after every change. Released rule files can be signed and checked when they load.

anywhere.title: One rule file, many places to run it
anywhere.desc: Use the CLI while you write rules, the server in production, or embed the engine in your program. The rule files are the same.

items.name: CLI
items.desc: Write rules, run tests and see what a change affects, on your machine. No Rust needed.

items.name: Server
items.desc: HTTP on 8080, gRPC on 50051, or a Unix socket. Multi-tenant, with versions and rollback.

items.name: Embedded
items.desc: Use ordo-core in a Rust program, or WebAssembly in the browser, with no server.

items.name: Decision model gateway
items.desc: Sits between your app and Jev, runs rules on the model's answers and logs every call so you can replay them before changing a threshold.
